newsitem.title: UK: Dollar stalls in Europe as FOMC keeps traders wary.
newsitem.headline: Dollar stalls in Europe as FOMC keeps traders wary.

text.p: The dollar ended little changed here as the U.S. Federal Reserve began the first of its two-day policy making meetings and finance ministers from the Group of Seven industrialised nations (G7) prepared to meet this weekend.
The U.S. unit was a touch softer against the mark and slightly firmer against the yen compared with Monday's close but did not stray far from 1.64 marks and 122 yen.

Analysts said the Fed's Open Market Committee (FOMC) was not expected to boost interest rates this week but the outside chance of a surprise move kept trading activity to a minimum and the dollar generally underpinned.
"We're unlikely to hear anything from the FOMC today and chances are pretty slim of a rate rise this week anyway," said Michael Burke, economist at Citibank.

Yet Burke says he believes that the dollar is just taking a breather before pushing higher again. The weekend G7 meeting is unlikely to put obstacles in the way of recent trends, whatever its opinion of the pace of dollar gains, he said.
"At the end of the day, the U.S. still seems fully committed to its strong dolar policy."
At 1605, the dollar was trading at 1.6412/22 marks compared with 1.6435/38 late Monday.
Against the yen, it was trading at 122.28/38 compared with 121.78/88 late yesterday.
The latest dollar/yen surge higher was checked last week amid rumours of Bank of Japan intervention and on concern the G7 may act to cap the dollar and possibly reverse its recent gains.
However, Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto said yesterday that this was not the current state of G7 thinking.

Bank of Japan (BOJ) governor Yasuo Matsushita today said it was desirable that currencies move in a stable manner. BOJ external reserves, however, fell in January for the first time in three years, suggesting the BOJ sold dollars, traders said.
Reserves fell $731 million in January from a month earlier to $217.14 billion.

The dollar/mark's rise, meantime, has been reined in over the past week by jitters in European peripheral markets like Spain and Italy, where an unwinding of extreme lira and peseta strength has given the mark a crutch against the dollar too.

The concerns in these markets have stemmed from a series of statements from German government officials, which suggest German opposition has hardened against anything other than a narrow group of core European countries starting monetary union.
These markets were calmer today too, however.

Dutch central bank president Wim Duisenberg, who is scheduled to become president of the European Monetary Institute this summer, said he expected all three Benelux countries, Germany, France, Austria, Finland and Ireland to start EMU on time on January 1, 1999.
However, he said it is "not a catastrophe if one, two, three, four countries join a little later" and he predicted that all 15 EU countries would be in EMU by 2002.
Elsewhere, the latest U.S. economic data was in line with expectations and gave little clue to FOMC deliberations.
